claims.text: All evaluated risk factors jointly accounted for 57.8% of global deaths in 2015.
All evaluated risk factors jointly accounted for 41.2% of global DALYs in 2015.
Global exposure to unsafe sanitation decreased by more than 25% between 1990 and 2015.
Global exposure to high body-mass index increased by more than 25% between 1990 and 2015.
High systolic blood pressure was the largest contributor to global DALYs among Level 3 risks in 2015, accounting for 211.8 million DALYs.
Smoking was the second largest Level 3 risk factor contributor to global DALYs in 2015, accounting for 148.6 million DALYs.

evidence.description: All risks jointly evaluated in 2015 accounted for 57·8% (95% CI 56·6–58·8) of global deaths.
All risks jointly evaluated in 2015 accounted for 41·2% (39·8–42·8) of DALYs.
Between 1990 and 2015, global exposure to unsafe sanitation, household air pollution, childhood underweight, childhood stunting, and smoking each decreased by more than 25%.
Global exposure for several occupational risks, high body-mass index (BMI), and drug use increased by more than 25% over the same period.
In 2015, the ten largest contributors to global DALYs among Level 3 risks were high systolic blood pressure (211·8 million [192·7 million to 231·1 million] global DALYs).
smoking (148·6 million [134·2 million to 163·1 million]) contributed to global DALYs in 2015.

methodologies.name: Comparative Risk Assessment (CRA) Framework
methodologies.description: A standardized framework to estimate attributable deaths, DALYs, and trends in risk factor exposure across time and geographies relative to theoretical minimum risk exposure levels.

methodologies.name: Summary Exposure Value (SEV)
methodologies.description: A metric calculated as the relative risk-weighted prevalence of exposure to enable comparison of exposure levels across dichotomous, polytomous, and continuous risk factors.

limitations.text: Relative risks were not systematically corrected for publication bias due to a lack of suﬃcient studies across all risk-outcome pairs.
Relative risks were generally assumed to be uniform across countries for a given age-sex group due to insuﬃcient evidence of geographic variation.
Proxies for exposure to some risk factors (such as zinc deficiency and occupational carcinogens) are coarse.
In previous GBD studies, comparable exposure metrics were not reported across all risk factors due to the complexity of quantifying polytomous and continuous risks.

future_work.text: Incorporate new risks including distal socioeconomic factors (such as educational attainment) and the absence of effective health interventions (such as vaccination or seat belts) in future iterations.
Develop avoidable burden estimates within the GBD framework by resolving issues around risk reversibility and appropriate counterfactual exposure distributions.
Evaluate new risk-outcome pairs for existing risk factors using expanded evidence bases.
